newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia heads for dry winter/spring - Met Bureau.
newsitem.headline: Australia heads for dry winter/spring - Met Bureau.

text.p: Large areas of eastern Australia were likely to be significantly drier than normal during the southern hemisphere winter and spring, Australia's Bureau of Meteorology said on Tuesday.
A strengthening El Nino weather pattern would persist for the rest of the year and was likely to become stronger, the head of the Bureau's national climate centre, Bill Kininmonth said.

"A continuation of the El Nino would have serious consequences for Australia," he said in a statement. "Large areas in eastern Australia are likely to be significantly drier than normal during winter and spring."
It was not possible to be precise about the parts of Australia which would be most affected because each El Nino event tended to portray unique characteristics, he said.

But regions most at risk of being significantly dry over winter (June to August) included most of eastern Australia, extending to Tasmania and South Australia, as well as parts of Western Australia, he said.

The main indicators of El Nino continued to strengthen in May, with the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean becoming warmer while trade winds across the western half of the Pacific remaining much weaker than normal, he said.
Also, the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), a measure of the cross-Pacific atmospheric pressure gradient, was still significantly negative, Kininmonth said.
"We can be quite confident ... that the El Nino pattern will persist for the remainder of the year and is likely to get stronger," he said.

Most El Nino events lasted about 12 to 15 months from autumn of one year to the autumn of the following year, while most computer models of the equatorial Pacific indicated continued warming of the sea surface temperature in central and eastern parts, he said.
The SOI gauges the difference in air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin. It is a measure of low level wind flows from the southern Pacific Ocean across to eastern Australia.

El Nino, which means "boy child" in Spanish, relates to warm water which appears off the South American coast near Peru and Ecuador, usually around Christmas, hence the name derived from that of the infant Christ.
Recent interest in El Nino has focused on patterns of ocean temperature across the tropical Pacific and the interaction between the ocean and the atmosphere.
An El Nino effect and current SOI patterns both suggest dry Australian weather.
Australia is moving into another big winter crop planting season but needs follow-up rain in many areas to support growing crops.
Wheat and barley are the main winter-grown crops in Australia.
